title: Determinants
summary: The determinant is the alternating multilinear function of the rows with det(I)=1. It multiplies over products, ignores transpose, changes sign when two rows are swapped, and vanishes exactly when the matrix is singular, which is exactly when 0 is an eigenvalue.
intuition:
The determinant is the function of a square matrix that measures signed volume. On the identity it equals $1$. It is linear in each row when the other rows are held fixed, and it changes sign when two rows are swapped. Those two sentences — multilinear and alternating — together with the value on $I$, determine the determinant completely. The same description works with columns instead of rows, which is why $\det(A^\top)=\det(A)$.

Multiplicativity is the structural fact used most often: $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$ for square matrices of the same size. Invertible matrices are exactly the ones with nonzero determinant, because $\det(A)\det(A^{-1})=\det(I)=1$. A product of many matrices therefore has determinant equal to the product of the determinants, and a single singular factor makes the whole product singular.

Singularity has two other names that examinations treat as the same statement. The matrix is singular, the determinant is zero, and $0$ is an eigenvalue. Each implies the others: $\det(A-\lambda I)$ at $\lambda=0$ is $\det A$, so the characteristic equation holds at $0$ exactly when the determinant vanishes, and that is exactly when the columns are dependent. The determinant is not linear as a function of the whole matrix. Row-by-row linearity does not give $\det(A+B)=\det(A)+\det(B)$.

definitions.body: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the rows of a square matrix that takes the value $1$ on the identity. Alternating means that swapping two rows changes the sign. Multilinear means linear in each row separately.
A square matrix is singular when it is not invertible. For a square matrix this is equivalent to $\det A=0$, to the columns being linearly dependent, and to $0$ being an eigenvalue.

Swapping two rows multiplies the determinant by $-1$. Adding a multiple of one row to a different row does not change the determinant. Multiplying a row by the scalar $c$ multiplies the determinant by $c$.

formulas.name: Product, transpose, eigenvalues
formulas.note: The product of eigenvalues counts algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$. $A$ and $B$ are square and the same size.

formulas.name: Zero determinant
formulas.latex: \det(A)=0\iff A\text{ is singular}\iff 0\text{ is an eigenvalue}
formulas.note: All three are statements about a square matrix. A non-square matrix has no determinant and no eigenvalues in this sense.

properties: The determinant is multilinear and alternating as a function of the rows, and also as a function of the columns. In particular $\det(A^\top)=\det(A)$.
$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$. Hence $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det(A)$ when $A$ is invertible, and $\det(A^k)=(\det A)^k$.
Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant. A matrix with two equal rows has determinant $0$.
$\det A=0$ if and only if $A$ is singular, if and only if $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.
For an $n\times n$ matrix, $\det(cA)=c^n\det(A)$. The exponent is $n$, not $1$.

examples.title: A product, a transpose, and a row swap
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\det A$, $\det B$, $\det(AB)$, and the determinant after swapping the two rows of $A$.
steps: $\det A=1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2$ and $\det B=2\cdot 3-0\cdot 1=6$. The product of these numbers is $-12$.

The product matrix is $AB=\begin{pmatrix}4&6\\10&12\end{pmatrix}$, and $\det(AB)=4\cdot 12-6\cdot 10=48-60=-12$, matching $\det(A)\det(B)$. Also $\det(A^\top)=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}=4-6=-2=\det A$.
Swap the rows of $A$ to get $\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $3\cdot 2-4\cdot 1=2$, which is $-\det A$.
examples.answer: $\det A=-2$, $\det B=6$, $\det(AB)=-12$, and swapping the rows of $A$ changes the determinant from $-2$ to $2$.

examples.title: A $3\times 3$ determinant and the eigenvalue $0$
examples.prompt: Compute $\det C$ for $C=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Then let $S$ be the matrix obtained by replacing the third row of $C$ with the first row, and relate $\det S$ to eigenvalues.
steps: Expand along the first row: $\det C=2\bigl(2\cdot 2-1\cdot 1\bigr)-1\bigl(1\cdot 2-1\cdot 0\bigr)+0=2(4-1)-(2)=6-2=4$.
The value $4$ is also the product of the eigenvalues of $C$. None of them is $0$, so $C$ is invertible.

The new matrix is $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\2&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its first and third rows agree, so the alternating property gives $\det S=0$. Thus $S$ is singular, and $0$ is an eigenvalue of $S$.
examples.answer: $\det C=4$, so $C$ is invertible and $0$ is not an eigenvalue. The matrix $S$ with two equal rows has determinant $0$ and has $0$ as an eigenvalue.

traps: Writing $\det(A+B)=\det A+\det B$. Row-by-row linearity is not linearity in the matrix. For $A=I$ and $B=I$ in size $2\times 2$, $\det(A+B)=\det(2I)=4$ while $\det A+\det B=2$.
Writing $\det(cA)=c\det A$ for an $n\times n$ matrix. The correct factor is $c^n$. Scaling one row by $c$ multiplies the determinant by $c$; scaling every row does it $n$ times.
Forgetting the sign of a row swap. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $2$, not $-2$, because it is $A$ above with the rows exchanged and $\det A=-2$.
Treating $\det A=0$ as a statement about the trace. A zero trace means the eigenvalues sum to zero. A zero determinant means one of them is zero.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def det2(M):
    return M[0][0] * M[1][1] - M[0][1] * M[1][0]

def det3(A):
    a, b, c = A
    return (
        a[0] * (b[1] * c[2] - b[2] * c[1])
        - a[1] * (b[0] * c[2] - b[2] * c[0])
        + a[2] * (b[0] * c[1] - b[1] * c[0])
    )

A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]]
assert det2(A) == -2
assert det2(B) == 6
assert det2(mul(A, B)) == -12
swapped = [A[1], A[0]]
assert det2(swapped) == 2
C = [[2, 1, 0], [1, 2, 1], [0, 1, 2]]
assert det3(C) == 4
print(4)

questions.stem: Swapping two rows of a square matrix
options: forces the determinant to be zero
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. The determinant is alternating: one transposition of rows multiplies it by $-1$. It becomes zero if the swap produces two equal rows, but a swap of two different rows does not by itself force a zero determinant. Adding a multiple of one row to another, which is not a swap, is the operation that leaves the determinant unchanged.

questions.stem: For a square matrix $A$, $\det A=0$ if and only if
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. The characteristic polynomial evaluated at $0$ is $\det A$, so $\det A=0$ exactly when $0$ is an eigenvalue, exactly when $A$ is singular. A symmetric matrix can have nonzero determinant, a zero trace does not force a zero eigenvalue, and an orthogonal matrix has determinant $\pm 1$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$ for square matrices of the same size.
$\det(A+B)=\det(A)+\det(B)$ for all square $A$ and $B$ of the same size.
The determinant is multilinear and alternating as a function of the rows.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. The determinant multiplies over products, is unchanged by transpose, and is defined by being multilinear and alternating on the rows with value $1$ on $I$. It is not additive: $\det(I+I)=\det(2I)=4$ for $2\times 2$ identity, while $\det I+\det I=2$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Compute $\det A=4-6=-2$ and $\det B=6-0=6$. Then $\det(AB)$ equals the product $(-2)(6)=-12$, and the explicit product $AB=\begin{pmatrix}4&6\\10&12\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $48-60=-12$. The transpose has the same determinant as $A$, so $\det(A^\top)=-2$, not $2$.
The answer is **4**. Expand along the first row: $2(4-1)-1(2-0)+0=2\cdot 3-2=4$. The same expansion is $2\cdot\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}-1\cdot\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$.
